questions.prompt:
(a) A mobile accessories retailer analyses six recent online orders to understand attachment behaviour around new smartphone purchases. The transaction log are shown in Table Q.1A.

The product codes map to real items as follows: a = Smartphone; b = Protective Case; c = Screen Protector; d = Power Bank; e = USB Cable.

| Transaction ID | Items |
| --- | --- |
| T1 | a, b, d, e |
| T2 | b, c, e |
| T3 | a, b, d, e |
| T4 | a, b, c, e |
| T5 | a, b, c, d, e |
| T6 | b, c, d |

(b) Derive all possible frequent k-itemsets with minimum support count=3 and following the Apriori property, list pruned itemsets at each stage.

(c) Generate a minimum of 5 possible association rules using the longest frequent k-itemsets and verify whether the generated rules are strong with the confidence threshold=60%.
questions.answer:
Frequent itemsets, with support counts:

- Singletons: a:4, b:6, c:4, d:4, e:5.
- Pairs: ab:4, ad:3, ae:4, bc:4, bd:4, be:5, ce:3, de:3.
- Triples: abd:3, abe:4, ade:3, bce:3, bde:3.
- Quadruple: abde:3.

Five strong rules from abde: abd → e:100%; abe → d:75%; ade → b:100%; bde → a:100%; ab → de:75%.
questions.explanation:
Count each itemset once per containing transaction. No singleton is pruned. Among all ten pairs, ac has count 2 and cd count 2, so both are removed.

All triples containing ac or cd are ruled out: abc, acd, ace, bcd, cde. With the usual lexicographic join of frequent pairs, bcd is generated then subset-pruned; the other four need not be generated. The surviving candidate triples are abd, abe, ade, bce and bde, and all meet the support threshold.

Joining abd and abe produces abde. Its four triples are frequent, and its support is 3, so it survives. Every other quadruple contains an infrequent pair. No further candidate can be joined from the single longest frequent itemset; the five-item set also contains infrequent pairs.

For a rule $X\Rightarrow Y$, confidence is $\operatorname{count}(X\cup Y)/\operatorname{count}(X)$. The five displayed rules have confidences $3/3$, $3/4$, $3/3$, $3/3$, and $3/4$. Each has support $3/6=50\%$, meeting the minimum support count 3, and confidence at least 60%. Thus all five are strong.

questions.prompt: A hospital laboratory claims that a new COVID testing kit correctly identifies infection 95% of the time. A researcher believes that the true accuracy is less than 95% and decides to test this claim at a 5% significance level. A random sample of n = 50 test results gives a sample mean accuracy of 0.93. The population standard deviation is known to be 0.04. At the 5% significance level, test whether the hospital laboratory's claim is justified. (critical value $Z_{0.05}=-1.645$).
questions.answer: $z=-3.5355$. Reject the null hypothesis; the data support accuracy below 95% under the stated known-standard-deviation model.
questions.explanation:
Use $H_0:\mu=0.95$ against $H_1:\mu<0.95$. The standard error is $0.04/\sqrt{50}=0.005657$. Therefore $z=(0.93-0.95)/(0.04/\sqrt{50})=-3.5355$. This is below the lower-tail cutoff -1.645, so reject the laboratory's claimed mean accuracy at the stated significance level.

The paper supplies a population standard deviation for a sample mean; this solution follows that model. A raw binary correct/incorrect test outcome would instead require a proportion model with a different standard error.

questions.prompt: Consider the scenario of mobile phone sales data, the mobile phone retailer analyzed monthly sales data over the period of 3 years. The data showed consistent upward movement due to market growth, with a little drop due to global electronic chip shortages. Identify the component of time series that represents the market growth, and name the time series component denote temporary drop?
questions.answer: Market growth is the trend component. The temporary shortage-related drop is an irregular component.
questions.explanation: A sustained long-run rise is a trend. A one-off external supply shock is irregular, rather than a fixed seasonal repetition. The question gives no evidence of a recurring multi-year business cycle, so the temporary drop should not automatically be labelled cyclical.

questions.prompt:
Per acre production data (in tons) for three varieties of wheat grown using four different fertilizers, each combination replicated twice, are given in Table Q. 2A. Test whether the variety differences and fertilizer differences are significant at 5% level.

| Variety | Replicate | Fertilizer 1 | Fertilizer 2 | Fertilizer 3 | Fertilizer 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Variety 1 | 1 | 8 | 9 | 6 | 10 |
| Variety 1 | 2 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 11 |
| Variety 2 | 1 | 7 | 8 | 5 | 9 |
| Variety 2 | 2 | 6 | 9 | 4 | 10 |
| Variety 3 | 1 | 10 | 11 | 8 | 12 |
| Variety 3 | 2 | 9 | 12 | 7 | 13 |
questions.answer: Variety F = 36.3333; fertilizer F = 47.5556. Both main effects are significant at the 5% level.
questions.explanation:
Use a replicated two-factor ANOVA with three varieties, four fertilizers and two observations per cell. Assume independent normal errors with common variance.

Grand mean is $8.6667$. Variety means are $8.5,7.25,10.25$; fertilizer means are $8.1667,9.5,6.1667,10.8333$.

| Source | Sum of squares | df | Mean square | F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Variety | 36.3333 | 2 | 18.1667 | 36.3333 |
| Fertilizer | 71.3333 | 3 | 23.7778 | 47.5556 |
| Interaction | 3.6667 | 6 | 0.6111 | 1.2222 |
| Within-cell error | 6.0000 | 12 | 0.5000 | — |
| Total | 117.3333 | 23 | — | — |

Compute variety SS as $4(2)\sum_i(\bar y_{i..}-\bar y)^2$ and fertilizer SS as $3(2)\sum_j(\bar y_{.j.}-\bar y)^2$. Error SS is the sum of squared deviations from each cell mean; each pair differs by one, giving $12(0.5)=6$. Interaction SS accounts for the remaining between-cell variation.

Divide each main-effect mean square by $MSE=0.5$. The upper-tail 5% critical values are approximately $F_{2,12}=3.8853$ and $F_{3,12}=3.4903$. Both observed F values exceed their cutoffs, so reject equal variety means and equal fertilizer means.

questions.prompt:
Suppose you have $L_1=\{I_1,I_2,I_3,I_4,I_5,I_6\}$ and the following transactions:

- $T_1:\{I_1,I_2,I_3,I_6\}$
- $T_2:\{I_2,I_4,I_5\}$
- $T_3:\{I_1,I_3,I_4,I_6\}$
- $T_4:\{I_2,I_3,I_5,I_6\}$
- $T_5:\{I_1,I_2,I_4,I_5\}$

Use the hash function $h(x,y)=((\operatorname{order}(x)\times11)+\operatorname{order}(y))\bmod10$.

(a) Construct the hash table for all 2-itemsets.

(b) Determine bucket counts.

(c) If min support = 4, specify which buckets are pruned and list the remaining candidate itemsets $C_2$.
questions.answer:
Bucket counts for buckets 0 through 9: 1, 1, 0, 2, 2, 4, 3, 6, 3, 5.

Retain buckets 5, 7, 9. Remaining hash-filtered candidates: {I1,I4}, {I2,I3}, {I1,I6}, {I2,I5}, {I3,I4}, {I3,I6}, {I4,I5}.
questions.explanation:
Use the smaller item index as x and the larger as y; $\operatorname{order}(I_j)=j$. A bucket count sums all pair occurrences hashed there, including collisions.

| Bucket | Pair and actual count | Bucket count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | {I4,I6}:1 | 1 |
| 1 | {I5,I6}:1 | 1 |
| 2 | None | 0 |
| 3 | {I1,I2}:2 | 2 |
| 4 | {I1,I3}:2 | 2 |
| 5 | {I1,I4}:2; {I2,I3}:2 | 4 |
| 6 | {I1,I5}:1; {I2,I4}:2 | 3 |
| 7 | {I1,I6}:2; {I2,I5}:3; {I3,I4}:1 | 6 |
| 8 | {I2,I6}:2; {I3,I5}:1 | 3 |
| 9 | {I3,I6}:3; {I4,I5}:2 | 5 |

Prune buckets 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 because their counts are below 4. A retained bucket does not prove each colliding pair frequent. In fact, none of these pairs has actual support count 4, so exact counting would produce an empty frequent-pair set.

The supplied $L_1$ is treated as the candidate-generating premise requested by the paper. Recomputing singleton frequency at threshold 4 would retain only I2; each of the other five items occurs three times. Thus the given L1 is inconsistent with that threshold.

questions.prompt:
Differentiate between Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE). Assume two model with given MAE and RMSE. Interpret the results and identify the better forecasting model. Justify your answer briefly.

- Model A: MAE = 5.2, RMSE = 6.8
- Model B: MAE = 4.9, RMSE = 5.0
questions.answer: Model B is better on both reported error measures, assuming both models are evaluated on the same observations and scale.
questions.explanation: MAE averages absolute errors and retains the original units. MSE averages squared errors, has squared units and penalizes large errors more heavily. RMSE is the square root of MSE and returns to the original units. Model B's lower MAE means smaller average absolute error; its lower RMSE also indicates better squared-error performance. Model A's larger gap between MAE and RMSE suggests greater variation in error magnitudes.

questions.prompt:
i) Find the elements of box plot using the following data: 78, 91, 68, 54, 82, 47, 60, 78, 97, 58, 62, 50, 50, 63, 92, 75 79, 63, 42, 61.

ii) Why is it sometimes necessary to create subsets from a large dataset before performing analysis?

iii) Measure the strength of the relationship between the ranks assigned by two different interviewers as shown below.

| Candidate | Interviewer 1 | Interviewer 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1 | 1 |
| B | 2 | 2 |
| C | 3 | 4 |
| D | 4 | 3 |
| E | 5 | 6 |
| F | 6 | 5 |
| G | 7 | 8 |
| H | 8 | 7 |
| I | 9 | 10 |
| J | 10 | 9 |
| K | 11 | 12 |
| L | 12 | 11 |

Transcription note: the paper omits the comma in “75 79”; these are treated as separate observations.
questions.answer:
Five-number summary = 42, 56, 63, 78.5, 97. IQR = 22.5; fences = 22.25, 112.25; outliers = 0.

Spearman rho = 0.9650, a strong positive rank association.
questions.explanation:
(i) Use the median-of-halves quartile convention. Sorted data: 42, 47, 50, 50, 54, 58, 60, 61, 62, 63, 63, 68, 75, 78, 78, 79, 82, 91, 92, 97. The median is the average of the middle pair, 63 and 63. The lower-half median is $(54+58)/2=56$ and upper-half median is $(78+79)/2=78.5$. Thus $IQR=78.5-56=22.5$ and the Tukey fences are $56-1.5(22.5)=22.25$ and $78.5+1.5(22.5)=112.25$. All observations lie within them, so whiskers reach 42 and 97. Other software quartile conventions can differ and should be stated.

(ii) Subsetting can reduce computation and memory needs, focus analysis on a relevant group, or create training and validation samples. Use representative sampling when generalizing to the full population; a convenient subset may be biased.

(iii) There are no tied ranks. The first two differences are zero; the other ten are either +1 or -1. Hence $\sum d_i^2=10$ and $\rho_s=1-6(10)/(12(12^2-1))=0.965034965\ldots$. The interviewers mostly agree.

questions.answer: Each of the three requested pairs has support count 3 and support 60%. All three pairs are frequent and maximal frequent.
questions.explanation: Each pair occurs in three of five transactions, so its support is $3/5=60\%$. Each singleton also occurs in four transactions and is frequent, but is not maximal because it has frequent pair supersets. The only triple has count 2 and support $40\%$, below the threshold. Therefore no frequent proper superset of any pair exists, making each requested pair maximal frequent.

questions.prompt: The sales of a retail store for five consecutive weeks are as follows: 100, 110, 95, 120, 130. Compute the 3-week moving average forecast for week 6. Interpret the whether this method would be appropriate if a strong upward trend continues.
questions.answer: Forecast = 115 units. A simple moving average will lag a continuing strong upward trend.
questions.explanation: The last three actual values are 95, 120 and 130. Their mean is $(95+120+130)/3=345/3=115$. The equal-weight moving average estimates a recent level and does not project the upward trend; a trend-aware method such as Holt's method is more appropriate if that trend persists.

questions.prompt:
Given the following transaction database:

| TID | Items |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | A, B, D |
| 2 | B, C, E |
| 3 | A, B, C, E |
| 4 | B, E |

(a) Using the FP-Growth algorithm, mine all frequent itemsets with a minimum support of 2.

- Construct the FP-tree.
- Show the conditional pattern bases and conditional FP-trees.
- List all frequent itemsets.

(b) State the advantages of the pattern growth approach over the Apriori algorithm.
questions.answer: Frequent itemsets with counts: A:2, B:4, C:2, E:3, AB:2, BC:2, BE:3, CE:2, BCE:2.
questions.explanation:
Singleton counts are B:4, E:3, A:2, C:2 and D:1. Remove D and order retained items B, E, A, C, breaking the equal-frequency tie alphabetically. Ordered transactions are [B,A], [B,E,C], [B,E,A,C], [B,E].

FP-tree, with child indentation:

- root
  - B:4
    - A:1
    - E:3
      - C:1
      - A:1
        - C:1

Conditional pattern bases and pruned conditional trees:

| Suffix | Conditional pattern base, with multiplicities | Conditional FP-tree |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C | [B,E]:1; [B,E,A]:1 | root → B:2 → E:2; A is below threshold |
| A | [B]:1; [B,E]:1 | root → B:2; E is below threshold |
| E | [B]:3 | root → B:3 |
| B | Empty prefix | Empty |

Mining C's conditional tree gives BC:2, CE:2 and BCE:2 in addition to C:2. Mining A's gives AB:2; mining E's gives BE:3. Include the frequent singletons to obtain the nine itemsets listed in the answer.

FP-growth avoids Apriori's large explicit candidate sets, compresses shared transaction prefixes, and uses two original-database scans before recursive conditional mining. It can still require substantial memory when the tree compresses poorly.

questions.prompt:
A beverage company tracks monthly sales (in units) of a new energy drink:

| Month | Sales |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 80 |
| 2 | 95 |
| 3 | 100 |
| 4 | 110 |
| 5 | 120 |

Using Single Exponential Smoothing (SES) with a smoothing constant $\alpha=0.4$, and assuming the forecast for Month 1 = 80 units,

(a) Calculate the forecast for Months 2 to 6.

(b) Compute the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for the forecasts from Months 2 to 5.
questions.answer: Forecasts for months two through six = 80, 86, 91.6, 98.96, 107.376 units. MAE = 17.11 units.
questions.explanation:
Use $F_{t+1}=0.4Y_t+0.6F_t$ without intermediate rounding.

| Forecast | Calculation | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| F2 | 0.4(80)+0.6(80) | 80 |
| F3 | 0.4(95)+0.6(80) | 86 |
| F4 | 0.4(100)+0.6(86) | 91.6 |
| F5 | 0.4(110)+0.6(91.6) | 98.96 |
| F6 | 0.4(120)+0.6(98.96) | 107.376 |

For months 2 through 5, absolute errors are $15,14,18.4,21.04$. Their sum is 68.44, so $MAE=68.44/4=17.11$. Do not include month 1's initialization or month 6's unknown actual in the error calculation.

questions.prompt:
A popular online bookstore analysed 800 customer purchase transactions and obtained the following data:

| Itemset | Number of Transactions |
| --- | --- |
| {Fiction Book} | 360 |
| {E-Reader} | 300 |
| {Fiction Book, E-Reader} | 180 |

(a) Calculate the pattern evaluation measures Lift and Kulc for the association rule: Fiction Book → E-Reader.

(b) Interpret what the obtained Lift and Kulc values indicate about the relationship between Fiction Book and E-Reader purchases.
questions.answer: Lift = 1.3333; Kulc = 0.55. Lift indicates positive association relative to independence; the average directional confidence is moderate.
questions.explanation:
$P(F)=360/800=0.45$, $P(E)=300/800=0.375$, and $P(F\cap E)=180/800=0.225$. Therefore lift is $0.225/(0.45\times0.375)=1.3333$, meaning co-purchase is about one-third more common than the independence baseline.

The directional confidences are $P(E\mid F)=180/360=0.5$ and $P(F\mid E)=180/300=0.6$. Kulczynski is their average, $(0.5+0.6)/2=0.55$. This is slightly above the course's neutral reference and far from perfect co-occurrence. Association does not establish causation.

questions.prompt:
A manufacturing unit tracks its quarterly production output. The data for the first four quarters are given below:

| Period (t) | Actual Production (Yt) |
| --- | --- |
| Q1 | 100 |
| Q2 | 120 |
| Q3 | 130 |
| Q4 | 150 |

Use smoothing constants =0.2 and =0.4. Applying Holt's Method

(a) Calculate the initial Level (L1) and Trend (T2).

(b) Calculate the Level (L2) and Trend (T3) for periods 2 and 3, respectively.

(c) Calculate the Forecast for period 4 (F4).

(d) Differentiate between Double and triple exponential smoothing techniques.

Transcription note: the paper omits the names of the smoothing constants and uses inconsistent trend subscripts. State the convention used.
questions.answer: Under the stated conventional initialization: initial level = 100; initial trend = 20; updated level for period two = 120; trend for period three = 19.2; forecast for period four = 157.2.
questions.explanation:
Assume the first constant is level smoothing $\alpha=0.2$ and the second is trend smoothing $\beta=0.4$. Initialize $L_1=Y_1=100$ and $T_1=Y_2-Y_1=20$. The paper calls the initial trend T2; here it is labelled T1, the trend available for forecasting period 2. The question does not specify this initialization, so a different explicitly stated convention can give a different forecast.

Use $L_t=\alpha Y_t+(1-\alpha)(L_{t-1}+T_{t-1})$, $T_t=\beta(L_t-L_{t-1})+(1-\beta)T_{t-1}$, and $F_{t+1}=L_t+T_t$.

For period 2: $L_2=0.2(120)+0.8(100+20)=120$, $T_2=0.4(120-100)+0.6(20)=20$.

For period 3: $L_3=0.2(130)+0.8(120+20)=138$, $T_3=0.4(138-120)+0.6(20)=19.2$.

Thus $F_4=138+19.2=157.2$. Q4's observed output is not used to forecast Q4.

Double exponential smoothing updates level and trend. Triple exponential smoothing also updates a seasonal component and is used when seasonality accompanies the level or trend.

questions.prompt:
A transaction database is given as follows:

| Transaction ID | Items Purchased |
| --- | --- |
| T1 | A, B, C |
| T2 | A, C, D |
| T3 | B, C, E |
| T4 | A, B, C, E |
| T5 | A, B, D, E |

(a) List all frequent itemsets having minimum support = 2.

(b) Identify the closed frequent itemsets and maximal frequent itemsets from the result.

(c) Explain why mining closed and max patterns is more efficient than mining all frequent itemsets.
questions.answer:
Frequent itemsets with counts: A:4, B:4, C:4, D:2, E:3, AB:3, AC:3, AD:2, AE:2, BC:3, BE:3, CE:2, ABC:2, ABE:2, BCE:2.

Closed frequent: A, B, C, AB, AC, AD, BC, BE, ABC, ABE, BCE.

Maximal frequent: AD, ABC, ABE, BCE.
questions.explanation:
Interpret the threshold as a support count, as indicated by the value 2. Count all singleton, pair and triple occurrences. No four-itemset reaches the threshold.

A frequent set is closed if no proper superset has equal support. D is not closed because AD has the same count 2; E is not closed because BE has count 3; AE is not closed because ABE has count 2; CE is not closed because BCE has count 2. Every other listed frequent set is closed.

A frequent set is maximal if no proper superset is frequent. The three frequent triples have no frequent larger supersets. AD has no frequent triple superset. All other frequent sets are contained in at least one of these four maximal sets.

Closed mining removes equal-support redundancy while preserving enough information to recover frequent-set supports. Maximal patterns compactly describe which subsets are frequent but lose their exact supports. Their smaller output and pruning opportunities can save time and storage, especially when long frequent patterns have many subsets.

questions.prompt: A data scientist is analysing the following cholesterol level (mg/dL) readings of 12 patients: [145, 155, 160, 162, 165, 172, 180, 190, 200, 220, 240, 260]. Apply equal-width and equal-frequency binning with 3 bins. Using histogram analysis, explain which binning approach (width-based or frequency-based) better represents the data distribution and why.
questions.answer: Equal-width bin width = 38.3333 mg/dL; counts = 7, 3, 2. Equal-frequency counts = 4, 4, 4.
questions.explanation:
For equal-width binning, the range is $260-145=115$, so width is $115/3=38.3333\ldots$. Use left-inclusive, right-exclusive intervals except that the final interval includes its right endpoint:

| Bin | Interval, approximate endpoints | Values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [145, 183.3333) | 145, 155, 160, 162, 165, 172, 180 |
| 2 | [183.3333, 221.6667) | 190, 200, 220 |
| 3 | [221.6667, 260] | 240, 260 |

For equal-frequency binning, sort and split the twelve observations into consecutive groups of four:

- First bin: 145, 155, 160, 162.
- Second bin: 165, 172, 180, 190.
- Third bin: 200, 220, 240, 260.

For displaying the distribution with ordinary frequency-bar heights, equal-width bins more directly show the concentration at lower values and the thinner right tail. Equal-frequency bins balance counts but have unequal widths; identical count heights can hide that shape. A properly normalized density histogram can also display unequal-width bins, so the choice is about the intended representation rather than one approach being universally better.
